\title{Checking a forecast put to Parliament: unbundling Canadian television, 2016--2019}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In April 2016 a House of Commons committee heard that new television rules from the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) would cost \lttvJobsTotal{} media jobs by 2020. It came from a commissioned study detailed enough to check. I compare the study's intermediate predictions with CRTC data for 2016--2019, under a plan fixed before collecting outcomes; total jobs and causal effects aren't tested. In pre-stated comparisons, specialty and pay channels' revenue, on which most of the job figure depends, came out smaller than the forecast, and distributors' revenue was consistent with it. The study assumed that \lttvByopSixteen{} of subscribers would take an entry-level package with chosen channels in 2016; the CRTC counted \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} by mid-2016, while a 2017 survey, outside the plan's sources, put starter-package adoption near the study's \lttvByopSeventeen{} for 2017. In later analyses, only a low uptake path among those tested keeps both revenue series compatible with a partial recalculation of the study's chain, and payments to Canadian channels per subscriber grew \lttvPerSubGrowth{}, against \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{} in its baseline. The testimony called an economy-wide estimate media jobs, described the study's 18\%, which its totals put at \lttvCPEShareTwenty{}, as a share of current spending, and omitted the uptake assumption.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} forecast evaluation; ex post analysis; economic impact studies; broadcasting regulation; Canada
